references.text: Abraham died and was gathered to his fathers ([ref:1 Mos 25:8|Genesis 25:8]). The expression 'Abraham's bosom' in Luke 16:22 refers to the idea of being gathered to one's ancestors after death, with Abraham as the foremost of the patriarchs.

The preceding context in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus ([ref:Luk 16:19-21|Luke 16:19-21]) describes the earthly lives of the two men—the rich man's extravagance and the poor man's misery—which form the background for the dramatic reversal that occurs in verse 22.

The continuation in [ref:Luk 16:23-26|Luke 16:23-26] describes the rich man's torment in Hades and his sight of Lazarus in Abraham's bosom, further elaborating on the contrasts between their two fates after death.

Jesus says that many will come and sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven ([ref:Matt 8:11|Matthew 8:11]). This shares the idea of fellowship with Abraham in the afterlife, parallel to 'Abraham's bosom'.

The expression about lying at someone's breast/bosom is used for the disciple who lay at Jesus' breast ([ref:Joh 13:23|John 13:23]). The Greek word "κόλπος" is used in both places and denotes a position of closeness and honor.
The angels who carry Lazarus away ([ref:Hebr 1:14|Hebrews 1:14]) correspond to the idea that angels are ministering spirits sent out to serve those who will inherit salvation.

The beatitude of the poor and the hungry ([ref:Luk 6:20-21|Luke 6:20-21]) reflects the same theme of an eschatological reversal where those who suffer in this life are comforted in the coming age—just as Lazarus was carried to Abraham's bosom.

In the parable of the rich farmer, God demands his soul back during the night ([ref:Luk 12:20-21|Luke 12:20-21]). The parallel to the rich man's death in 16:22 emphasizes that wealth cannot protect against death or secure a good fate afterward.

The psalmist writes: "God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will take me" ([ref:Sal 49:16|Psalm 49:16]). This expresses the hope that God will take the righteous to himself after death, just as Lazarus was carried to Abraham's bosom.

In the parable of the sheep and the goats, Jesus separates the righteous from the unrighteous ([ref:Matt 25:32-33|Matthew 25:32-33]). The same final separation between the righteous and the unrighteous is seen in the fates of Lazarus and the rich man.
